abandon.e: From Middle English abandounen, from Old French abandoner, formed from a (“at, to”) + bandon (“jurisdiction, control”), from Late Latin bannum (“proclamation”), bannus, bandum, from Frankish *ban, *bann, from Proto-Germanic *bannaną (“to proclaim, command”) (whence English ban), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂- (“to speak”).
abandon.g: To give up or relinquish control of, to surrender or to give oneself over, or to yield to one's emotions.

abandon.e: From Middle English abandoun, from Old French abandon, from Old French abondonner.
abandon.g: A yielding to natural impulses or inhibitions; freedom from artificial constraint, with loss of appreciation of consequences. (Now especiall

abandoned.e: From Middle English abandoned, equivalent to abandon + -ed.
abandoned.g: Having given oneself up to vice; immoral; extremely wicked, or sinning without restraint; irreclaimably wicked.

abase.e: From Late Middle English abaishen, abashen, abaisse, abassen, abesse, abessen (“to be upset; to embarrass; to surprise; to confound; to bend down, stoop; to abase, degrade, disgrace”), from Middle French abaisser, from Old French abaissier, abessier (“to prostrate oneself.
abase.g: To lower, as in condition in life, office, rank, etc., so as to cause pain or hurt feelings; to degrade, to depress, to humble, to humiliate

abate.e: From Middle English abaten, from Anglo-Norman abatre, from Late Latin abbattere, from Latin battere. detailed etymology, sense derivation, and cognates The verb is derived from Middle English abaten (“to demolish, knock down; to defeat, strike down; to strike or take down (a sail); to throw down; to bow dejectedly or submissively; to be dejected; to stop.
abate.g: To lessen (something) in force or intensity; to moderate.

abate.e: From Anglo-Norman abatre, probably an alteration of Anglo-Norman and Middle French embatre, enbatre (“to drive or rush into; to enter into a tenement without permission”) (compare Late Latin abatare).
abate.g: To enter upon and unlawfully seize (land) after the owner has died, thus preventing an heir from taking possession of it.

abide.e: From Middle English abyden, from Old English ābīdan (“to abide, wait, remain, delay, remain behind; survive; wait for, await; expect”), from Proto-West Germanic *uʀbīdan, from Proto-Germanic *uzbīdaną (“to expect, tolerate”), equivalent to a- + bide. The sense of pay for is due to influence from aby.
abide.g: To endure without yielding; to withstand.

abiding.e: Present participle or participial adjective from abide (verb) + -ing; or, from Middle English participle form of abiden, abyden (“to abide”).
abiding.g: Continuing or persisting in the same state: lasting, enduring; steadfast.

ability.e: From Middle English abilite (“suitability, aptitude, ability”), from Old French ableté, from Latin habilitās (“aptness, ability”), from habilis (“apt, fit, skillful, able”); equivalent to able + -ity.

abject.e: PIE word h₂epó The adjective is derived from Late Middle English abiect, abject (adjective), from Middle French abject (modern French abject, abjet (obsolete)), and from its etymon Latin abiectus (“abandoned; cast aside”), an adjective use of the perfect passive participle of abiciō (“to discard, throw away”).
abject.g: Existing in or sunk to a low condition, position, or state; contemptible, despicable, miserable.

abject.e: From Late Middle English abjecten (“to cast out, expel”), from abiect, abject (adjective) (see etymology 1). Sense 3 (“of a fungus: to give off (spores or sporidia)”) is modelled after German abschleudern (“to give off forcefully”).
abject.g: To cast off or out (someone or something); to reject, especially as contemptible or inferior.

ablaze.g: Burning fiercely; in a blaze; on fire.

able.e: From Middle English ablen, from Middle English able (adjective).

aboard.e: From Middle English abord, from a- (“on”) + bord (“board, side of a ship”); equivalent to a- + board.
aboard.g: On board; into or within a ship or boat; hence, into or within a railway car.

abode.e: From Middle English abod, abad, from Old English *ābād, related to ābīdan (“to abide”); see abide. For the change of nouns, compare abode, preterite of abide.

abolish.e: From late Middle English abolisshen, from Middle French aboliss-, extended stem of abolir, from Latin abolēre (“to retard, check the growth of, (and by extension) destroy, abolish”), and inchoative abolēscere (“to wither, vanish, cease”).
abolish.g: To end a law, system, institution, custom or practice.

abominable.e: From Middle English abhomynable, from Old French abominable, from Late Latin abōminābilis (“deserving abhorrence”), from abōminor (“abhor, deprecate as an ill omen”), from ab (“from, away from”) + ōminor (“forebode, predict, presage”), from ōmen (“sign, token, omen”).
abominable.g: Worthy of, or causing, abhorrence, as a thing of evil omen; odious in the utmost degree; very hateful; detestable; loathsome; execrable.

abomination.e: From Middle English abominacioun, from Middle French abomination (“horror, disgust”), from Late Latin abōminātiō, abōminātiōnem (“abomination”) Doublet of abominatio.
abomination.g: An abominable act; a disgusting vice; a despicable habit.

abound.e: From Middle English abounden, abounde, from Old French abonder, abunder, from Latin abundāre (“overflow”), which comes from ab (“from, down from”) + undō (“surge, swell, rise in waves, move in waves”), from unda (“wave”).
abound.g: To be full to overflowing; to bristle.

about.e: Preposition and adverb from Middle English aboute, abouten, from Old English abūtan, onbūtan, from on (“in, on”) + būtan (“outside of”) (compare modern English but, bout), itself from be (“by”) + ūtan (“outside”); equivalent to on + be + out or on + but. Not related to bout (“period of time”) Adjective from Middle English about (adverb).
about.g: In a circle around; all round; on every side of; on the outside of; around.

above.e: From Middle English above, aboven, abuven, from Old English ābufan, onbufan, from on (“on”) + bufan (“over”), (akin to Icelandic ofan (“from above”), Middle Dutch bōven, Old Frisian bova, Middle High German bobene) from bī (“by”) + ufan (“over”); also cognate with Danish oven, Dutch boven, German oben, Swedish ovan, Old Saxon oƀan, Old High German obana.
above.g: Physically over; on top of; worn on top of, said of clothing.

abroad.e: From Middle English abrood (“broadly widely scattered”), from a- (“on, in”) + brood (“broad”). Equivalent to a- + broad.
abroad.g: Beyond the bounds of a country; in foreign countries.

absence.e: From Middle English absence, from Old French absence, ausence, from Latin absentia, from absēns (“absent”), present active participle of absum (“to be away or absent”), from ab (“from, away from”) + sum (“to be”).
absence.g: A state of being away or withdrawn from a place or from companionship

absent.e: From Middle English absent, from Middle French absent, from Old French ausent, and their source, Latin absens, present participle of absum (“to be away from”), from ab (“away”) + sum (“to be”).
absent.g: Being away from a place; withdrawn from a place; existing but not present; (sometimes) missing.

absent.e: From Middle English absenten, from Old French absenter, from Late Latin absentāre (“keep away, be away”).

absolute.e: From Middle English absolut, from Middle French absolut, from Latin absolūtus (“unconditional; unfettered; completed”), perfect passive participle of absolvō (“loosen, set free, complete”), from ab (“away”) + solvo (“to loose”). Influenced in part by Old French absolu.
absolute.g: Free of restrictions, limitations, qualifications or conditions; unconditional.

absolutely.e: From late Middle English absolutly, equivalent to absolute + -ly.
absolutely.g: In an absolute or unconditional manner; utterly, positively, wholly.

absolve.e: From Middle English absolven, from Latin absolvere (“set free, acquit”), from ab (“away from”) + solvō (“loosen, free, release”).
absolve.g: To set free, release or discharge (from obligations, debts, responsibility etc.).

absorb.e: From Middle French absorber, from Old French assorbir, from Latin absorbeō (“swallow up”), from ab- (“from”) + sorbeō (“suck in, swallow”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *srebʰ- (“to sip”).
absorb.g: To include so that it no longer has separate existence; to overwhelm; to cause to disappear as if by swallowing up; to incorporate; to assim

abstain.e: From Middle English absteynen, absteinen, abstenen, from Old French astenir, abstenir, from Latin abstineō (“to hold oneself back”) from abs- (“from”) + teneō (“to hold”).

abstinence.e: From Middle English abstinence, from Old French abstinence, from Latin abstinentia, from abstinēns, present participle of abstineō (“to withhold”). Equivalent to abstain + -ence.
abstinence.g: The act or practice of abstaining, refraining from indulging a desire or appetite.

abundance.e: From Middle English abundaunce, habaundance, from Old French habundance, abondance, from Latin abundantia (“fullness, plenty”), from abundō (“to overflow”). Equivalent to abound + -ance.

abundant.e: From Middle English abundaunt, habundaunt, aboundant, from Anglo-Norman abundant, from Old French abondant, from Latin abundāns, present participle of abundō (“to overflow, to abound”).
abundant.g: Fully sufficient; found in copious supply; in great quantity; overflowing.

abundantly.e: From Middle English abundantly, abundauntli, habundantly, habundauntliche, equivalent to abundant + -ly.
abundantly.g: In an abundant manner; in a sufficient degree; in large measure.

abuse.e: From Middle English abusen, then from either Old French abus (“improper use”), or from Latin abūsus (“misused, using up”), perfect active participle of abūtor (“make improper use of, consume, abuse”), from ab (“away”) + ūtor (“to use”). Equivalent to ab- + use.
abuse.g: Improper treatment or usage; application to a wrong or bad purpose; an unjust, corrupt or wrongful practice or custom.

abuse.e: From Middle English abusen, from Middle French abuser, from Latin abūsus (“misused, using up”), perfect active participle of abūtor (“to use up, misuse, consume”), from ab (“from, away from”) + ūtor (“to use”).
abuse.g: To put to a wrong use; to misapply; to use improperly; to use for a wrong purpose or end; to pervert

abusive.e: From French abusif, from Latin abūsīvus, from abusus + -ivus (“-ive”). Equivalent to abuse + -ive.
abusive.g: Prone to treat someone badly by coarse, insulting words or other maltreatment; vituperative; reproachful; scurrilous.
